newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BTR profits fall, but shares rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BTR profits fall, but shares rise.

text.p: Industrial conglomerate BTR Plc on Thursday reported 1996 profits fell 13.4 percent, but shares climbed as investors believed the widely diversified group was making good progress on getting its act together.
BTR, which embarked on a massive restructuring programme in September, saw pre-tax profit fall to 1.301 billion pounds ($2.10 billion) last year from 1.501 billion in 1995.
The result was better than expected and BTR boosted market confidence further by forecasting steady underlying improvement in 1997.
"The results confirm that we are delivering against our strategy that we announced last year," chief executive Ian Strachan said, adding BTR's reorganisation was on schedule.
To improve cash flow, BTR is weeding out underperforming activities, while focusing on its top industrial manufacturing and engineering operations.
Most of the continuing businesses performed better in 1996, but the improvement was offset by specific factors such as an 11 percent fall in 1996 profits in the automotive sector, BTR said.
But Strachan forecast the automotive division's results would pick up this year as start-up problems in North America were overcome.
Meanwhile, BTR's shares rose 8-1/2 pence to 261 in late morning trade.
"The results and statement are reasonably upbeat, the stock has already had a bit of a recovery and it could go further," said one dealer.
"Having been a real dog it is starting to look a bit better," he added.

Dealers said the shares were also supported by BTR's comment it had no need for additional equity. The company said it might even be advantageous to purchase some warrants or shares, but added no full-blown share buy-back programme was planned.
But BTR, which has over 1,000 businesses across the globe, does plan to sell about two dozen more firms -- mostly smaller ones -- to complete its divestment drive by the end of the year.
BTR has already sold off operations representing 1.75 billion pounds of 1995 sales against a 2.3 billions pound target by the end of 1997.
Last year's sales included the Dunlop Slazenger sports business, the Tilcon Aggregates activities in the U.S. and the Electric Power Group along with some 30 smaller businesses.
Strachan said the pound's current strength would fail to have a significant impact on 1997 results as most of BTR's transactions are handled in other currencies than sterling.
Last year's result would have been hit by 50 million pounds if the currency had been trading at current levels for the whole year.

While profits in the automotive division fell in 1996, they rose nine percent in the power drives sector and increased by 10 and one percent respectively in process control and the packaging and materials division.
Profits in specialist engineering rose three percent.
In the building products and polymeric products divisions results were respectively up two and down 12 percent.
